extracted.intended_audience: technology transfer professionals, university TTOs, small business and nonprofit contractors, IP managers, research administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and compliance standards under the Bayh‑Dole Act for nonprofit organizations and small business contractors concerning title, patenting, licensing, commercialization, reporting, and agency march‑in rights for federally funded inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor petition to retain title
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may petition the funding agency to allow the inventor to retain title to the subject invention; the decision lies solely with the funding agency, which must consult with the small business or nonprofit organization prior to making its determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor is granted the right to retain title, the inventor remains obligated to Bayh‑Dole elements that protect U.S. government interest (e.g., file appropriate patent applications, provide preference to U.S. industries and small businesses). Bayh‑Dole does not provide accommodations to the small business/nonprofit if an inventor retains title (the organization may not have a license back unless the government retains title). Institutions should consider policies requiring inventors who obtain title to grant at least research rights back to the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing of patent applications — U.S. timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The small business or nonprofit organization must file its initial patent application on subject inventions it elects to retain title within one year after election of title or, if earlier, prior to the end of any statutory period wherein valid U.S. patent protection can be obtained after a publication, sale, or public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations must monitor statutory bars and election timelines closely; failure may permit the funding agency to take title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing of patent applications — foreign timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications in additional countries or international patent offices must be filed within either ten months of the corresponding initial patent application, or no longer than six months after the date the commissioner of patents and trademarks grants permission to file foreign patent applications when such filing was previously prohibited by a secrecy order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal funding agencies may grant extensions at their discretion. All patent applications and issued patents must cite that the invention was made using federal funds and that the U.S. government has certain rights (example citation provided in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of discontinuing prosecution and agency title-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: If the organization determines not to continue prosecution of a patent application or the payment of maintenance fees or defense in reexamination/opposition, written notice of such determination must be provided to the funding agency within thirty days before the expiration of the response period required by the relevant patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The funding agency may take title in countries where the organization fails to file timely or decides not to continue prosecution/maintenance/defense. If title is conveyed to the funding agency, the small business/nonprofit will retain a nonexclusive, royalty‑free license worldwide (extends to domestic subsidiaries and affiliates) and may only be transferred with agency approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. government license to practice subject inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bayh‑Dole Act requires the automatic granting to the U.S. government of a nonexclusive, nontransferable, irrevocable, paid‑up license to practice or have practiced on its behalf throughout the world any subject invention to which a small business or nonprofit organization has elected to retain title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This license lets government researchers use the technology royalty‑free and permits a contractor to produce the subject invention for government use. Third parties (contractors, grantees, cooperative funding recipients) can use the government's license only when granted authority for a specific contract or need. The government is not entitled to automatic price discounts merely because it holds such a license. The government's rights attach only to inventions created by federally funded research and may not extend to later inventions based on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of utilization, commercialization, and public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The nonprofit organization or small business must promote the utilization, commercialization, and public availability of those inventions in which title is retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding agencies may request periodic reports no more frequently than annually on utilization and efforts to promote utilization. Reports should include status of development, date of first commercial sale/use, gross royalties received, and any other reasonably specified data.

rubrics_metrics.name: License terms to ensure commercialization (development obligations)
rubrics_metrics.description: License agreements should include provisions to ensure licensed inventions are developed and brought to market and allow monitoring of licensee performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended provisions: development section requiring licensee intent to develop commercial products; warranties; obligations to provide development reports; licensor audit rights; termination penalties for failure to actively pursue development, provide timely reports, or for slow market introduction. These prevent 'shelving' by licensees and allow enforcement of Bayh‑Dole commercialization obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for United States industry (domestic manufacture requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations receiving title are precluded from granting exclusive rights to use or sell any subject invention in the United States unless the licensee agrees that products embodying the invention will be manufactured substantially in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirement may be waived in individual cases where reasonable but unsuccessful efforts were made to grant licenses on similar terms to potential domestic licensees, or where domestic manufacture is not commercially feasible. The assistant secretary of commerce may review licensing programs for compliance and recommend changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on assignment by nonprofit organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonprofit organizations are precluded from assigning any rights in a subject invention without the approval of the funding agency, except assignment to an organization whose primary function is management of inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft license agreements carefully to ensure they are not, in effect, assignments. Evaluate agreements based on rights conveyed (not labels). Excessive rights granted to a licensee may be construed as an assignment in violation of Bayh‑Dole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding assignment — retain sufficient rights
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid an agreement being construed as an assignment, licensors should retain sufficient rights and consider specific reserved rights and termination provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested provisions: reserve rights to allow other nonprofit research institutions and government agencies to use licensed inventions for noncommercial research; include termination for failure to commercialize; preclude licensee assignment without written consent; maintain the right to bring infringement actions. Case law (Waterman, Vaupel, Abbott) shows courts look at what rights were retained to determine whether a transfer was an assignment or a license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue distribution and inventor royalty sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonprofit organizations are required to share royalties with inventors of the subject invention, including federal employee co‑inventors when the funding agency deems appropriate; Bayh‑Dole does not specify exact amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions typically outline royalty distribution formulas in IP policies and often do not distinguish between federally and non‑federally funded inventions. 'Royalty' is broadly interpreted to include license fees, royalties on product sales, revenue from sale of stock, and in limited situations contributions. After payment of expenses (including payments to inventors and patent prosecution/enforcement costs), remaining revenues must be used to support research or education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for small business licensees
rubrics_metrics.description: The nonprofit organization must make reasonable efforts, under the circumstances, to attract small‑business licensees and to give a preference to a small business if it determines the small business's plan is equally likely to bring the invention to practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key considerations: whether the small business has capability and resources to carry out its plan; what constitutes 'reasonable efforts' depends on nature, duration, and expense needed to bring invention to market. The preference is discretionary and not intended to preclude rights of first refusal or other arrangements with larger firms in certain cases. The assistant secretary of commerce for technology policy may review and recommend changes to licensing policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: March‑in rights — statutory grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal funding agency has the right to require the organization, assignee, or exclusive licensee to grant a nonexclusive, partially exclusive, or exclusive license in any field of use to a responsible applicant if the agency determines one of specified conditions exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory grounds include: (1) necessary action has not been taken or is not expected to be taken within a reasonable time to achieve practical application; (2) action is necessary to alleviate health or safety needs not reasonably satisfied; (3) action is necessary to meet public use requirements not reasonably satisfied; (4) action is necessary because the obligation to provide a preference for U.S. industries has not been obtained or waived, or because an exclusive licensee is in breach. If contractor/assignee/licensee refuses, the agency may grant the license itself. Historical examples (CellPro petition; NIH Norvir inquiries) illustrate agency analyses and the high bar for exercising march‑in.

rubrics_metrics.name: March‑in procedures and required notices/comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Before initiating march‑in proceedings, the agency must notify the organization in writing of the information and request informal written or oral comments; procedural timelines are specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no comments within 30 days, the agency may proceed. If comments are received (or later if agency hasn't initiated procedures), the agency must within 60 days either initiate procedures or notify the organization it will not pursue march‑in on the available information. The formal march‑in notice must state the reasons, facts, specify field(s) of use considered, and advise the organization's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical application means to manufacture in the case of a composition or product, to practice in the case of a process or method, or to operate in the case of a machine or system; in each case under such conditions as to establish that the invention is being utilized and that its benefits are, to the extent permitted by law or government regulations, available to the public on reasonable terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited regulation: 37 C.F.R. 401.2(e). This definition is central to analyses of commercialization, march‑in, and preference decisions.
